quotes.quote: An investment firm's edge is built deal by deal, but the judgment behind each decision usually lives in the heads of a few senior investors.
the firm may keep the documents, but it loses the reasoning.
Terminal X's Capital Memory operating system is designed to pay that debt down.

GPT‑6.1 Sol helped the Eval Agent catch about 25% more recommendations that strayed from a fund's mandate and ran the same workflows at approximately 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model.
Across 500 scored judgments, its Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol agreed with the senior human reviewer 88.6% of the time, vs. 86.4% for the next-best model, an improvement of 220 basis points.
The Eval Agent checks each output against a 54-criterion rubric.
It asks: Are the numbers, comps, consensus figures, and quotes pulled from the right sources? Does the narrative hold? Does the recommendation tie to the house view?
Each check scores pass or fail. Every fail includes a one-line reason and a better source or corrected text and becomes a Memory.

Terminal X engineers spend weeks onsite with the customer, reverse-engineering the firm's trusted memos and capturing processes that were never written down, such as how the credit desk screens a borrower or which sources the co-investment team pulls before a memo.
Next, those processes are encoded in hundreds of agents, customized by asset class and strategy, with sub-agents for each investment stage.
GPT‑6.1 Sol handles the stages that require judgment and a huge context window: synthesizing the investment thesis, identifying key considerations, and assessing fit with the firm's mandate.
The agents work inside each firm's private data room, a dedicated environment for enterprises to share and manage sensitive investment data.
The agents process documents in English, Korean, Japanese, and Chinese

Engineers turn each Memory into a repeatable workflow on Terminal X's platform, where every production query is auditable with its full trail: the steps taken, sources retrieved, model used, and the reasoning.

According to Terminal X, customers see significant savings as a result of this approach, including one private equity firm that reported $2.4 million in annualized savings from automated due diligence and investment memo workflows.
It's an orchestrated workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol and other OpenAI models designed to read every agent output the way a VP reads an analyst's work.
Every answer gets eval'd, and whatever the analyst corrects teaches the system a little more about how that firm works,
Terminal X picks models based on its own evaluation results.
The Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol caught about 25% more of these departures than the next-best model did.
GPT‑6.1 Sol's token efficiency on long-context work enabled Terminal X to build a deeper review workflow within the same budget.
That deeper review flagged deals that a single pass on a comparable model had waved through.
GPT‑6.1 Sol also ran the same workflows at about 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model, at similar speed.
Using GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, Terminal X has built 1,700 firm Memories, run more than 1 million custom workflows, and reached a weekly active user count equal to 81% of its monthly active users.
Terminal X's next step is to extend firm Memories from desks to individuals, so that each investment professional's standard is captured as it is practiced, not only as it is described.
The firms that win the next decade will own their judgment as data. Our job is to make that judgment measurable, so it can be kept, improved, and reused.

We benchmarked three AI platforms (ChatGPT 5.0, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Pro) across 500 natural language financial queries from real retail investors and compared their performance to Terminal X across 7 key categories.
Responses were evaluated across seven dimensions by a team of independent human evaluators.
Terminal X achieved a 89.9% composite accuracy score, outperforming the next best general purpose chatbot by +19.3 percentage points.
We ran 22 models through 259 graded runs on 9 evals that cover every stage of our pipeline.
Eval sets range from 19 to 28 cases each, 214 cases in all, built from real investment workflows.
They stay private, so every score reflects a model seeing the work for the first time.
